in-class7

Geography of Accessibility · Catchment methods for eldercare in Singapore

Author

Zhenhua Liu

Published

October 18, 2026

1. Study question and reproducibility

How does the choice of catchment method change modelled access to eldercare in Singapore? This exercise follows the supplied In-class Exercise 7 slides, covering nearest-facility distance, 2SFCA, E2SFCA, Gaussian KD2SFCA, 3SFCA and M2SFCA. All maps and numerical results below are generated by the R code, with independent calculations used to check the package outputs.

The related Hands-on Exercise 7 uses different accessibility models. This page implements the classroom’s catchment workflow and its five floating catchment variants.

Package installation is separate from analysis. The setup pins catchment to revision b96fb58adcd0e476cbb634aeb6ce27981fbc1dc3; the executed session information records the installed versions. Input provenance and checksums accompany the analysis.

2. Import and prepare the teaching data

The subzones, hexagons, eldercare locations and OD matrix come from the instructor’s pinned teaching repository. Spatial layers use SVY21 / Singapore TM, EPSG:3414. The code repairs invalid polygons, checks feature identifiers, and verifies a complete OD table with no duplicated pairs.

Note

Each hexagon receives demand 100 and each facility capacity 100, following the classroom scenario. These are illustrative assumptions. The boundaries and facility records are historical; the results describe the teaching dataset and cannot establish current service shortages. Raw inputs remain local, with acquisition instructions provided.

manifest <- read_csv("in-class7/data/input-checksums.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(unname(tools::md5sum(file.path("in-class7/data/raw", manifest$file))), manifest$md5))
read_layer <- function(name) {
  st_read(file.path("in-class7/data/raw/geospatial", paste0(name, ".shp")), quiet = TRUE) |>
    st_transform(3414) |> st_make_valid()
}
mpsz <- read_layer("MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL")
hexagons <- read_layer("hexagons") |> select(fid) |> rename(id = fid) |> mutate(demand = 100)
eldercare <- read_layer("ELDERCARE") |> select(fid) |> mutate(capacity = 100)
ODMatrix <- read_csv("in-class7/data/raw/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(hexagons) == 3125, nrow(eldercare) == 120, nrow(mpsz) == 323,
  !anyDuplicated(hexagons$id), !anyDuplicated(eldercare$fid),
  nrow(ODMatrix) == nrow(hexagons) * nrow(eldercare),
  !anyDuplicated(ODMatrix[c("origin_id", "destination_id")]),
  setequal(ODMatrix$origin_id, hexagons$id), setequal(ODMatrix$destination_id, eldercare$fid),
  all(is.finite(ODMatrix$total_cost)), all(ODMatrix$total_cost > 0),
  all(st_is_valid(hexagons)), all(st_is_valid(mpsz)), st_crs(hexagons)$epsg == 3414)
knitr::kable(tibble(dataset = c("Subzones", "Demand hexagons", "Eldercare facilities", "OD pairs"),
  records = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(hexagons), nrow(eldercare), nrow(ODMatrix))))
dataset records

Align the distance matrix by feature ID

The OD costs are road-network distances in metres, not travel times. I rename the long-table columns to from_id, to_id and dist, then explicitly match rows to demand hexagons and columns to facilities. Dividing by 1,000 converts the catchment calculations to kilometres. A successful pivot alone does not guarantee the correct feature order.

ODMatrix_tidied <- ODMatrix |> transmute(from_id = origin_id, to_id = destination_id,
                                        dist = total_cost)
wide <- ODMatrix_tidied |> pivot_wider(names_from = to_id, values_from = dist)
wide <- wide[match(hexagons$id, wide$from_id), ]
distmat_km <- as.matrix(wide[, as.character(eldercare$fid)]) / 1000
dimnames(distmat_km) <- list(as.character(hexagons$id), as.character(eldercare$fid))
stopifnot(!anyNA(distmat_km), all(is.finite(distmat_km)),
  identical(rownames(distmat_km), as.character(hexagons$id)),
  identical(colnames(distmat_km), as.character(eldercare$fid)))
knitr::kable(tibble(origins = nrow(distmat_km), destinations = ncol(distmat_km),
                    minimum_km = min(distmat_km), maximum_km = max(distmat_km)), digits = 3)
origins destinations minimum_km maximum_km
3125 120 0.037 56.351

3. Distance to the closest eldercare facility

With active accessibility, opportunities belong to the destination facilities. I supply facility IDs and capacity to cost_to_closest(), rather than treating origin demand as destination opportunities. With positive capacity at every facility, the result should equal each origin’s minimum OD distance; the code verifies that equality before joining results by id.

# Active accessibility uses opportunities at destinations: supply belongs to facilities.
facility_land_use <- st_drop_geometry(eldercare) |> transmute(id = fid, capacity)
dist2closest <- cost_to_closest(travel_matrix = ODMatrix_tidied,
  land_use_data = facility_land_use, opportunity = "capacity", travel_cost = "dist",
  n = 1, group_by = character(0), active = TRUE, fill_missing_ids = TRUE)
hex_acc <- hexagons |> left_join(dist2closest |> rename(nearest_m = dist), by = "id")
hex_acc$nearest_km <- hex_acc$nearest_m / 1000
stopifnot(nrow(hex_acc) == nrow(hexagons),
  isTRUE(all.equal(hex_acc$nearest_km, unname(apply(distmat_km, 1, min)))))
nearest_summary <- tibble(minimum_km = min(hex_acc$nearest_km),
  median_km = median(hex_acc$nearest_km), maximum_km = max(hex_acc$nearest_km),
  cells_beyond_5km = sum(hex_acc$nearest_km > 5))
knitr::kable(nearest_summary, digits = 3)
minimum_km median_km maximum_km cells_beyond_5km
0.037 4.064 32.45 1281

Network distance to the nearest teaching-data facility. Darker orange indicates a longer distance; red points are facilities.

access_map <- function(field, title, distance = FALSE) {
  value <- hex_acc[[field]]
  positive <- value[value > 0]
  breaks <- unique(as.numeric(quantile(positive, seq(0, 1, length.out = 8))))
  labels <- paste(formatC(head(breaks, -1), format = "g", digits = 3),
                  formatC(tail(breaks, -1), format = "g", digits = 3), sep = " to ")
  classes <- as.character(cut(value, breaks, labels = labels, include.lowest = TRUE))
  if (any(value == 0)) {
    classes[value == 0] <- "0 (outside catchment)"
    labels <- c("0 (outside catchment)", labels)
  }
  plot_data <- hex_acc
  plot_data$map_class <- factor(classes, levels = labels, ordered = TRUE)
  stopifnot(!anyNA(plot_data$map_class))
  palette <- colorRampPalette(if (distance) c("#fff7ec", "#7f2704") else c("#f7fbff", "#08306b"))(length(labels))
  tm_shape(plot_data) + tm_polygons(fill = "map_class",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = palette),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = if (distance) "Distance (km)" else "Supply / demand", text.size = 0.7),
    col = "white", lwd = 0.1) +
    tm_shape(eldercare) + tm_dots(size = 0.17, fill = "#bd4734", col = "white") +
    tm_title(title) + tm_compass(type = "arrow", size = 1.5) + tm_scalebar() +
    tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)
}
access_map("nearest_km", "Distance to the nearest eldercare facility", distance = TRUE)

The median nearest distance is 4.064 km. 1281 hexagons are more than 5 km from their closest facility. Distance measures proximity but does not account for competition for supply.

4. Two-step floating catchment area: 2SFCA

For each facility, I divide its capacity by the demand within its catchment. For each hexagon, I then sum the ratios of reachable facilities. At a 5 km threshold, eligible origin–destination pairs receive equal weight:

\[R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_i P_i w_{ij}}, \qquad A_i = \sum_j w_{ij}R_j.\]

Here \(S_j\) is capacity, \(P_i\) is demand, and \(w_{ij}\) defines the selected catchment. Scores represent modelled supply per unit demand. I follow the slides’ max_cost = 5 call, retaining the package’s boundary convention.

hex_acc$FCA2 <- catchment_ratio(consumers = hexagons$demand,
  providers = eldercare$capacity, cost = distmat_km, max_cost = 5)
access_map("FCA2", "2SFCA: 5 km catchment")

5. Enhanced 2SFCA: stepped distance decay

The classroom weights are 1, 0.4, 0.1, 0.05 and 0.01 for the successive 0–1, 1–2, 2–3, 3–4 and 4–5 km bands, and zero beyond 5 km. Nearer pairs therefore contribute more to both competing demand and allocated supply. The matrix validation below checks the actual band membership.

step_weights <- list(c(5, .01), c(4, .05), c(3, .1), c(2, .4), c(1, 1))
hex_acc$E2SFCA <- catchment_ratio(consumers = hexagons$demand,
  providers = eldercare$capacity, cost = distmat_km, weight = step_weights)
access_map("E2SFCA", "E2SFCA: stepped distance decay")

6. Gaussian kernel-density 2SFCA

I use weight = "gaussian" with the package default scale made explicit as 2 km. The slides do not specify a maximum distance for this model, so the Gaussian tail remains untruncated. This differs from the 5 km kernel calculation on the hands-on page; their scores should not be treated as interchangeable.

hex_acc$KD2SFCA <- catchment_ratio(consumers = hexagons$demand,
  providers = eldercare$capacity, cost = distmat_km, weight = "gaussian", scale = 2)
access_map("KD2SFCA", "Gaussian KD2SFCA: scale = 2 km, untruncated")

7. Three-step floating catchment area: 3SFCA

The normalize_weight = TRUE option adjusts the stepped weights for provider choice. Inspection of the pinned package implementation shows that its effective weight is \(w_{ij}^2 / \sum_j w_{ij}\), used in both demand and supply steps. This page reproduces that implementation and checks it explicitly; it is not simply a row-normalized weight matrix.

hex_acc$FCA3 <- catchment_ratio(consumers = hexagons$demand,
  providers = eldercare$capacity, cost = distmat_km, weight = step_weights,
  normalize_weight = TRUE)
access_map("FCA3", "3SFCA: selection-adjusted stepped weights")

8. Modified 2SFCA: M2SFCA

M2SFCA retains stepped weights for competing demand but squares the weights on the provider-allocation side. Distant supply is penalized further. Consequently, its demand-weighted total need not equal total capacity, so its absolute scores require separate interpretation.

hex_acc$M2SFCA <- catchment_ratio(consumers = hexagons$demand,
  providers = eldercare$capacity, cost = distmat_km, weight = step_weights,
  adjust_providers = function(w) w^2)
access_map("M2SFCA", "M2SFCA: squared provider-side weights")

9. Validate and compare results

The following checks reconstruct each method from dense weight matrices independently of catchment_ratio(). They verify finite non-negative scores and numerical agreement for every hexagon. For the four models using the same weights on both sides, the demand-weighted allocation must recover total capacity. M2SFCA is excluded from that conservation assertion because its supply-side weights differ.

# Independent dense calculations verify all five package outputs.
D <- distmat_km
binary <- 1 * (D < 5)
stepped <- matrix(0, nrow(D), ncol(D))
for (step in step_weights) stepped[D <= step[1]] <- step[2]
gaussian <- exp(-D^2 / (2 * 2^2))
selection <- stepped^2 / pmax(rowSums(stepped), 1e-100)
manual <- function(demand_weight, supply_weight = demand_weight) {
  denominator <- colSums(demand_weight * hexagons$demand)
  denominator[abs(denominator) < .Machine$double.eps] <- 1
  as.vector(supply_weight %*% (eldercare$capacity / denominator))
}
manual_results <- list(FCA2 = manual(binary), E2SFCA = manual(stepped),
  KD2SFCA = manual(gaussian), FCA3 = manual(selection), M2SFCA = manual(stepped, stepped^2))
methods <- names(manual_results)
validation <- bind_rows(lapply(methods, function(method) {
  value <- hex_acc[[method]]
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(value) & value >= 0),
    isTRUE(all.equal(value, manual_results[[method]], check.attributes = FALSE)))
  tibble(method, max_absolute_error = max(abs(value - manual_results[[method]])),
    demand_weighted_total = sum(value * hexagons$demand),
    zero_access_cells = sum(value == 0))
}))
stopifnot(all(abs(validation$demand_weighted_total[validation$method != "M2SFCA"] -
  sum(eldercare$capacity)) < 1e-6))
knitr::kable(validation |> mutate(max_absolute_error = formatC(max_absolute_error, format = "e", digits = 2)), digits = 3)
method max_absolute_error demand_weighted_total zero_access_cells
FCA2 0.00e+00 12000.000 1281
E2SFCA 0.00e+00 12000.000 1281
KD2SFCA 5.00e-16 12000.000 0
FCA3 3.89e-16 12000.000 1281
M2SFCA 0.00e+00 4251.595 1281

Distributions and rank agreement

Each map uses its own positive-score quantiles. This reveals spatial patterns but means colours cannot be compared as equal numerical intervals across maps. The table and boxplots retain the original score units; rank correlations compare ordering without assuming the methods have equal scales.

scores <- st_drop_geometry(hex_acc) |> select(id, nearest_km, all_of(methods))
summary_results <- scores |> pivot_longer(all_of(methods), names_to = "method", values_to = "access") |>
  group_by(method) |> summarise(minimum = min(access), median = median(access),
    mean = mean(access), maximum = max(access), zero_access_cells = sum(access == 0), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(summary_results |> mutate(across(c(minimum, median, mean, maximum),
  ~ formatC(.x, format = "g", digits = 4))))
method minimum median mean maximum zero_access_cells
E2SFCA 0 0.003798 0.0384 0.7445 1281
FCA2 0 0.02073 0.0384 0.9314 1281
FCA3 0 0.005286 0.0384 0.8188 1281
KD2SFCA 2.356e-57 0.01062 0.0384 0.3977 0
M2SFCA 0 4.465e-05 0.01361 0.5064 1281

Distributions of modelled access across the 3,125 equal-demand hexagons.

Distributions of modelled access across the 3,125 equal-demand hexagons.

long <- scores |> pivot_longer(all_of(methods), names_to = "method", values_to = "access")
ggplot(long, aes(x = method, y = access)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "#b9d9e8", outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Modelled supply per unit demand", title = "Comparing catchment methods",
    caption = "Each hexagon has equal demand. Zero access is retained.")

At 5 km, 2SFCA has 1281 zero-access hexagons. E2SFCA, 3SFCA and M2SFCA use the same 5 km support, so they identify the same excluded cells. The untruncated Gaussian model has 0 zero scores. A small positive Gaussian score does not imply practically convenient access.

The Spearman correlation between 2SFCA and E2SFCA is 0.958, while E2SFCA and 3SFCA correlate at 0.995. These observed differences show how distance decay and choice adjustment affect location rankings.

Planning-region comparison

I dissolve subzones into planning regions and assign each hexagon to its largest overlapping region. Each hexagon contributes once, avoiding duplicated boundary cells. These are equal-cell summaries under the assumed equal demand, not population-weighted estimates.

regions <- mpsz |> select(REGION_N) |> group_by(REGION_N) |> summarise()
# Intersect only geometry: do not split and repeat accessibility attributes.
overlap <- st_intersection(st_geometry(hex_acc), st_geometry(regions))
indices <- attr(overlap, "idx")
assignment <- tibble(cell = indices[, 1], region = indices[, 2],
  area = as.numeric(st_area(overlap))) |>
  group_by(cell) |> slice_max(area, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> ungroup()
regional_hex <- hex_acc
regional_hex$REGION_N <- regions$REGION_N[assignment$region[
  match(seq_len(nrow(hex_acc)), assignment$cell)]]
stopifnot(nrow(regional_hex) == nrow(hex_acc))
regional_hex$REGION_N[is.na(regional_hex$REGION_N)] <- "OUTSIDE BOUNDARY"
regional_summary <- regional_hex |> st_drop_geometry() |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(methods), names_to = "method", values_to = "access") |>
  group_by(REGION_N, method) |> summarise(cells = n(), median = median(access),
    mean = mean(access), zero_access_cells = sum(access == 0), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(regional_summary |> mutate(across(c(mean, median), ~ formatC(.x, format = "g", digits = 4))))

The region(s) with the highest median score across these model summaries are CENTRAL REGION. Regional medians conceal local pockets of weak access, so the maps remain necessary alongside the table.

Catchment sensitivity

I repeat basic 2SFCA at 3, 5 and 8 km. This isolates the hard distance threshold while holding facilities, demand and capacity fixed.

sensitivity <- bind_rows(lapply(c(3, 5, 8), function(cutoff) {
  value <- catchment_ratio(hexagons$demand, eldercare$capacity, distmat_km, max_cost = cutoff)
  tibble(catchment_km = cutoff, zero_access_cells = sum(value == 0), median = median(value),
    rank_correlation_to_5km = cor(value, hex_acc$FCA2, method = "spearman"))
}))
knitr::kable(sensitivity, digits = 4)
catchment_km zero_access_cells median rank_correlation_to_5km
3 1963 0.0000 0.7995
5 1281 0.0207 1.0000
8 788 0.0284 0.8553 
write_csv(scores, "in-class7/results/accessibility-by-hexagon.csv")
write_csv(summary_results, "in-class7/results/model-summary.csv")
write_csv(regional_summary, "in-class7/results/regional-summary.csv")
write_csv(validation, "in-class7/results/validation.csv")
write_csv(sensitivity, "in-class7/results/catchment-sensitivity.csv")
write_csv(nearest_summary, "in-class7/results/nearest-summary.csv")
write_csv(as.data.frame(rank_correlations) |> tibble::rownames_to_column("method"),
  "in-class7/results/rank-correlations.csv")

The 3 km scenario excludes 1963 cells; the 8 km scenario excludes 788. A larger catchment changes both reachable supply and competing demand, so individual scores need not rise monotonically as the threshold expands.

10. Reflection

Nearest distance answers a proximity question. Floating catchment methods additionally model competing demand, and the decay and allocation rules change which locations rank well. I would report the model assumptions and sensitivity results alongside any map, then replace the synthetic demand and capacity with observed older-resident counts and service places before making planning recommendations. Walking conditions, transport mode, service eligibility, cross-boundary options and network provenance would also need investigation.

## 1. Study question and reproducibility

How does the choice of catchment method change modelled access to eldercare in Singapore? This exercise follows the supplied [In-class Exercise 7 slides](https://isss626-ay2026-27aug.netlify.app/in-class_ex/in-class_ex07/in-class_ex07-accessibility), covering nearest-facility distance, 2SFCA, E2SFCA, Gaussian KD2SFCA, 3SFCA and M2SFCA. All maps and numerical results below are generated by the R code, with independent calculations used to check the package outputs.

The related [Hands-on Exercise 7](../handson7/index.qmd) uses different accessibility models. This page implements the classroom's **catchment** workflow and its five floating catchment variants.

```{r}
#| label: c7-packages
```

To reproduce from the `ISSS626-GAA.Rproj` project root in RStudio:

```{r}
#| eval: false
source("in-class7/R/install-packages.R") # first use only
source("in-class7/R/download-data.R")
system2("quarto", c("render", "in-class7/index.qmd"))
```

Package installation is separate from analysis. The setup pins catchment to revision `b96fb58adcd0e476cbb634aeb6ce27981fbc1dc3`; the executed session information records the installed versions. [Input provenance](data/README.md) and [checksums](data/input-checksums.csv) accompany the analysis.

## 2. Import and prepare the teaching data

The subzones, hexagons, eldercare locations and OD matrix come from the instructor's [pinned teaching repository](https://github.com/tskam/IS415/tree/acaa1f9995d3d778a02a09c6bbdd5ef4f4eae773/Hands-on_Ex/Hands-on_EX11/data). Spatial layers use **SVY21 / Singapore TM, EPSG:3414**. The code repairs invalid polygons, checks feature identifiers, and verifies a complete OD table with no duplicated pairs.

::: {.callout-note}
Each hexagon receives demand **100** and each facility capacity **100**, following the classroom scenario. These are illustrative assumptions. The boundaries and facility records are historical; the results describe the teaching dataset and cannot establish current service shortages. Raw inputs remain local, with acquisition instructions provided.
:::

```{r}
#| label: c7-inputs
```

### Align the distance matrix by feature ID

The OD costs are road-network **distances in metres**, not travel times. I rename the long-table columns to `from_id`, `to_id` and `dist`, then explicitly match rows to demand hexagons and columns to facilities. Dividing by 1,000 converts the catchment calculations to kilometres. A successful pivot alone does not guarantee the correct feature order.

```{r}
#| label: c7-matrix
```

## 3. Distance to the closest eldercare facility

With active accessibility, opportunities belong to the **destination facilities**. I supply facility IDs and capacity to `cost_to_closest()`, rather than treating origin demand as destination opportunities. With positive capacity at every facility, the result should equal each origin's minimum OD distance; the code verifies that equality before joining results by `id`.

```{r}
#| label: c7-nearest
#| fig-cap: "Network distance to the nearest teaching-data facility. Darker orange indicates a longer distance; red points are facilities."
```

The median nearest distance is **`r round(median(hex_acc$nearest_km), 3)` km**. **`r sum(hex_acc$nearest_km > 5)` hexagons** are more than 5 km from their closest facility. Distance measures proximity but does not account for competition for supply.

## 4. Two-step floating catchment area: 2SFCA

For each facility, I divide its capacity by the demand within its catchment. For each hexagon, I then sum the ratios of reachable facilities. At a 5 km threshold, eligible origin–destination pairs receive equal weight:

$$R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_i P_i w_{ij}}, \qquad A_i = \sum_j w_{ij}R_j.$$

Here $S_j$ is capacity, $P_i$ is demand, and $w_{ij}$ defines the selected catchment. Scores represent modelled supply per unit demand. I follow the slides' `max_cost = 5` call, retaining the package's boundary convention.

```{r}
#| label: c7-2sfca
#| fig-cap: "2SFCA with a 5 km catchment. Zero access is a separate legend class."
```

## 5. Enhanced 2SFCA: stepped distance decay

The classroom weights are **1, 0.4, 0.1, 0.05 and 0.01** for the successive 0–1, 1–2, 2–3, 3–4 and 4–5 km bands, and zero beyond 5 km. Nearer pairs therefore contribute more to both competing demand and allocated supply. The matrix validation below checks the actual band membership.

```{r}
#| label: c7-e2sfca
#| fig-cap: "E2SFCA using the five distance bands from the supplied slides."
```

## 6. Gaussian kernel-density 2SFCA

I use `weight = "gaussian"` with the package default scale made explicit as **2 km**. The slides do not specify a maximum distance for this model, so the Gaussian tail remains untruncated. This differs from the 5 km kernel calculation on the hands-on page; their scores should not be treated as interchangeable.

```{r}
#| label: c7-kd2sfca
#| fig-cap: "Gaussian KD2SFCA with a 2 km scale and no hard catchment cutoff."
```

## 7. Three-step floating catchment area: 3SFCA

The `normalize_weight = TRUE` option adjusts the stepped weights for provider choice. Inspection of the pinned [package implementation](https://github.com/uva-bi-sdad/catchment/blob/b96fb58adcd0e476cbb634aeb6ce27981fbc1dc3/R/catchment_ratio.R) shows that its effective weight is **$w_{ij}^2 / \sum_j w_{ij}$**, used in both demand and supply steps. This page reproduces that implementation and checks it explicitly; it is not simply a row-normalized weight matrix.

```{r}
#| label: c7-3sfca
#| fig-cap: "3SFCA using the package's selection-adjusted stepped weights."
```

## 8. Modified 2SFCA: M2SFCA

M2SFCA retains stepped weights for competing demand but squares the weights on the provider-allocation side. Distant supply is penalized further. Consequently, its demand-weighted total need not equal total capacity, so its absolute scores require separate interpretation.

```{r}
#| label: c7-m2sfca
#| fig-cap: "M2SFCA with squared provider-side weights."
```

## 9. Validate and compare results

The following checks reconstruct each method from dense weight matrices independently of `catchment_ratio()`. They verify finite non-negative scores and numerical agreement for every hexagon. For the four models using the same weights on both sides, the demand-weighted allocation must recover total capacity. M2SFCA is excluded from that conservation assertion because its supply-side weights differ.

```{r}
#| label: c7-validation
```

### Distributions and rank agreement

Each map uses its own positive-score quantiles. This reveals spatial patterns but means colours cannot be compared as equal numerical intervals across maps. The table and boxplots retain the original score units; rank correlations compare ordering without assuming the methods have equal scales.

```{r}
#| label: c7-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Distributions of modelled access across the 3,125 equal-demand hexagons."
```

At 5 km, 2SFCA has **`r sum(hex_acc$FCA2 == 0)` zero-access hexagons**. E2SFCA, 3SFCA and M2SFCA use the same 5 km support, so they identify the same excluded cells. The untruncated Gaussian model has **`r sum(hex_acc$KD2SFCA == 0)` zero scores**. A small positive Gaussian score does not imply practically convenient access.

The Spearman correlation between 2SFCA and E2SFCA is **`r round(rank_correlations["FCA2", "E2SFCA"], 3)`**, while E2SFCA and 3SFCA correlate at **`r round(rank_correlations["E2SFCA", "FCA3"], 3)`**. These observed differences show how distance decay and choice adjustment affect location rankings.

### Planning-region comparison

I dissolve subzones into planning regions and assign each hexagon to its largest overlapping region. Each hexagon contributes once, avoiding duplicated boundary cells. These are equal-cell summaries under the assumed equal demand, not population-weighted estimates.

```{r}
#| label: c7-regions
```

The region(s) with the highest median score across these model summaries are **`r paste(unique(best_regions$REGION_N), collapse = ", ")`**. Regional medians conceal local pockets of weak access, so the maps remain necessary alongside the table.

### Catchment sensitivity

I repeat basic 2SFCA at 3, 5 and 8 km. This isolates the hard distance threshold while holding facilities, demand and capacity fixed.

```{r}
#| label: c7-sensitivity
```

The 3 km scenario excludes **`r sensitivity$zero_access_cells[sensitivity$catchment_km == 3]`** cells; the 8 km scenario excludes **`r sensitivity$zero_access_cells[sensitivity$catchment_km == 8]`**. A larger catchment changes both reachable supply and competing demand, so individual scores need not rise monotonically as the threshold expands.

## 10. Reflection

Nearest distance answers a proximity question. Floating catchment methods additionally model competing demand, and the decay and allocation rules change which locations rank well. I would report the model assumptions and sensitivity results alongside any map, then replace the synthetic demand and capacity with observed older-resident counts and service places before making planning recommendations. Walking conditions, transport mode, service eligibility, cross-boundary options and network provenance would also need investigation.
